Al-Baydawi's commentary on Surah 26, verses 4–6:

﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them from the sky a sign,﴾ a manifest proof compelling them to faith, or a calamity that forces them to it. ﴿So their necks would remain humbled before it,﴾ submissive (*munqadin*). Its original form is *fa-ẓallū lahā khāḍiʿīn* (فَظَلُّوا لَها خاضِعِينَ), but *al-aʿnāq* (الأعناق, "the necks") was inserted (*fa-uqḥimat*, فَأُقْحِمَتِ) to specify the place of the humbling, and the predicate was left in its original form.

It has also been said that when the necks were described with the attributes of rational beings, they were treated as though they were rational beings (*ujriyat majrāhum*). It has also been said that what is meant by the necks is the leaders or the groups, from the saying of the poet:

*jāʾanā ʿunuqun mina al-nās li-fawjin minhum*
("There came to us a neck of people, for a company of them.")

It is also read *khāḍiʿatan* (خاضِعَةً). *Ẓallat* (ظَلَّتْ) is coordinated with *nunazzil* (نُنَزِّلْ) by the coordination of *wa-akun* (وَأكُنْ) upon *fa-aṣṣaddaq* (فَأصَّدَّقَ), because if it were said *anzalnā* (أنْزَلْنا) instead of it, it would be correct.

﴿And there does not come to them any reminder﴾ — an admonition or a portion of the Qur'an — ﴿from the Most Merciful﴾ — which He reveals to His Prophet — ﴿newly revealed﴾ — its revelation being renewed, for the repetition of admonition and the variation of affirmation. ﴿except that they turn away from it﴾ — except that they renew their aversion from it and their persistence in what they were upon.

﴿So they have indeed denied﴾ — that is, they denied the reminder after their aversion, and they went to excess in denying it, to the extent that it led them to mock it. This is implicitly indicated in His saying, ﴿so there will come to them﴾ — that is, when the punishment of God touches them on the day of Badr or on the Day of Resurrection — ﴿the news of that at which they used to mock﴾: whether it was true or false, and whether it was worthy of being believed and of its importance being magnified, or of being denied and its matter being made light of.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 7–9:

﴿Have they not looked at the earth﴾: have they not considered its wonders? ﴿How many pairs of every noble kind﴾ We have caused to grow therein: "kind" (ṣinf). (p-134)

"Noble" (karīm): praiseworthy, abundant in benefit. It is a description applicable to everything that is commended and found pleasing. Here it may be understood as restricting what implies the evidence of power, or as clarifying and alerting that there is no plant except that it has a benefit, either by itself or together with something else. ("Every" [kull]) indicates the encompassing of the pairs, and ("how many" [kam]) indicates their abundance.

﴿Surely in that﴾: surely in the growing of those kinds, or in each one of them. ﴿is a sign﴾ indicating that the One who causes them to grow is perfect in power and wisdom, and abundant in favour and mercy. ﴿Yet most of them are not believers﴾: in the knowledge and decree of God; therefore such mighty signs do not benefit them.

﴿And surely your Lord, He is the Mighty﴾: the Victorious, capable of exacting retribution from the disbelievers. ﴿the Merciful﴾: in that He granted them respite; or, "the Mighty" in His retribution against those who disbelieve, and "the Merciful" toward whoever repents and believes.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 10–11:**

﴿And when your Lord called Moses﴾ is governed by an implied verb, *udhkur* (remember), or it is an adverbial clause (*zarf*) modifying what follows. ﴿That come﴾: meaning *ti* (come), or *bi-anni* (with *anni*) *'it'* (come).

﴿the wrongdoing people﴾: in disbelief, in enslaving the Children of Israel, and in slaughtering their sons.

﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾ is either a substitute (*badal*) for the first phrase or an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to it. The restriction to "the people" alone may be because it is known that Pharaoh was more deserving of this description. ﴿Will they not fear God?﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*), which Moses' being sent to them to warn them follows, as a cause of wonder at their excess in wrongdoing and their audacity against Him. It is also read with the *ta'* (*a-la yattaqun* as *a-la tattaqun*) as a shift of person (*iltifat*) toward them, as rebuke and anger against them. Although they were absent at that time, they are treated as present in the speech addressed to them by the sender (God), insofar as he (Moses) conveys it to them and makes them hear it at the start of their hearing. Along with this there is greater urging toward piety for whoever reflects on it and considers its source. It is also read with the *kasra* on the *nun* (*ittaqini*), dispensing with the *ya'* of possession (*ya' al-idafa*). It may also mean "O people, fear Me," like His saying: "Ala ya asjudu" (Will you not prostrate?).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 12–14:

﴿He said, "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me, and my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be freed, so send [revelation] to Harun."﴾ He ordered the request that his brother be joined to him and made a partner with him in the matter upon three things: the fear of being denied, the constriction of the heart from being affected by it, and the increase of the impediment in the tongue through the contraction of the spirit into the inner part of the heart when it is constricted, so that it is not freed. For when these come together, there is the need for a helper who strengthens his heart and takes his place whenever an impediment afflicts him, so that his call is not disrupted and his proof is not cut off. This is not a pretext from him, nor a hesitation in receiving the command; rather it is a seeking of what would be an aid in carrying it out and a paving of the way for his excuse in it. Ya'qub read ﴿and my breast will be constricted﴾ and ﴿and my tongue will not be freed﴾ in the accusative, coordinating them with ﴿they will deny me﴾, so that they are among the things he feared.

﴿And they have a charge against me﴾, i.e., a consequence of a sin, so the noun was omitted or the thing was named by its name. What is meant is the killing of the Qibti, and he called it a sin only according to their claim. This is a summary of his story, which is elaborated in several places. ﴿So I fear that they will kill me﴾ on account of it before conveying the message. This too is not a pretext; rather it is a seeking of protection from the anticipated calamity, just as that request was a seeking of support and assistance in the matter of the call. And his saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 15–17:

﴿He said, "Never! So go, both of you, with Our signs."﴾ In response to him, granting his two requests with His promise to remove the calamity they feared, which would surely deter him from fear, and to include his brother with him in the mission. The address in ﴿fa-dhhaba﴾ (so go) is in the masculine dual imperative form by *taghlib* (giving precedence to the present party, the addressee), because it is conjoined to the verb implied by the context.

﴿Never!﴾ It is as if it were said: "Be restrained, O Musa, from what you suppose. Go, you and the one you requested." ﴿Indeed, We are with you﴾ meaning Musa, Harun and Fir'awn (Pharaoh). ﴿listening﴾ hearing what passes between you and him, so I will make you prevail over him. He, exalted is He, depicted Himself as one present at a dispute among a people, listening to what passes among them and watching for the reinforcement of His allies from among them, as an exaggeration in the promise of help. For this reason he used the word "listening," which means attending (*al-istima'*), metaphorically for hearing (*al-sam'*), which means the general perception of letters and sounds. This is a second predicate, or the predicate alone, and ﴿with you﴾ is superfluous.

﴿So come to Fir'awn and say, "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ He used the singular *rasul* (messenger) because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) described by the word, as it is shared between the sender and the message. The poet said:

"The slanderers have lied; I did not disclose to them a secret, nor did I send them with a messenger."

For this reason it is used in the dual at times and in the singular at others. Or (it is singular) because the two are united in brotherhood, or because of the unity of the sender and what is sent. Or because he intended that each one of us is a messenger.

﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾ meaning, send, since the word *rasul* includes the meaning of sending, which in turn includes the meaning of saying. The intended meaning is: release them so that they may go with us to al-Sham (Greater Syria).

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 23–25:**

﴿Pharaoh said: And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ When he heard the answer to what he had criticised, and saw that he did not desist by it, he began to object to his claim, starting by inquiring about the reality of the one sent.

﴿He said: Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ He made Him known by His most evident attributes and effects, since individuals cannot be defined except by mentioning attributes and actions. To this He alluded with His words:

﴿If you are certain﴾, i.e., if you are certain of things, verifying them, you know that these sensible bodies are contingent (mumkin) because of their composition, their multiplicity, and the change of their states. Therefore they have a necessary originator (mubdi' wajib), one that is necessary in its own essence (wajib li-dhatihi). That originator must be the origin of all the other contingents, whether it is possible to perceive them or not. Otherwise it would entail a plurality of Necessary Existents, or the independence of some contingents from it, and both are impossible. Then that Necessary Existent cannot be defined except through its external properties, because definition by its essence is impossible, and definition by what is internal to it is impossible, because composition in its essence is impossible.

﴿He said to those around him: Do you not listen?﴾ His answer: he asked him about his reality, and he mentioned his actions. Or [Pharaoh] claims that he is the Lord of the heavens, and they are necessary and self-moving by their essence, as is the doctrine of the Dahriyya (those who deny a Creator and hold that time and matter are eternal). Or [Pharaoh's claim is] that it is not known that they need an influencer.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 26, verses 26–28:

﴿He said, "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers of old."﴾ This is a shift to something about which such a doubt cannot arise, and about whose need for a wise Fashioner no one could be uncertain. It is also closer to the observer and clearer upon reflection.

﴿He said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman."﴾ He (Pharaoh) would ask him about one thing and he would answer about another. He called him "messenger" in mockery.

﴿He said, "Lord of the East and the West and whatever is between them."﴾ You witness every day that He brings the sun from the East and moves it along an orbit different from the orbit of the day before, until He brings it to the West, in a beneficial manner by which the affairs of creation are ordered. ﴿If you have understanding﴾: if you have intellect, you would know that there is no answer for you beyond this. He first spoke to them gently, then, when he saw the severity of their obstinacy (*shakimah*), he spoke to them harshly and opposed them with the same kind of speech they had used.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 29–30:

﴿He said: "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned."﴾ This is a shift from debate to threat, after argument had failed him; such is the habit of the stubborn one who has been refuted. It has been used as evidence that he claimed divinity and denied the Creator, and that his amazement at the words ﴿Will you not listen?﴾ was at the attribution of lordship to someone other than himself. Perhaps he was a dahri (one who holds that time alone causes everything, a materialist), who believed that whoever possesses a land or takes charge of its affairs by the power of his star deserves worship from its people. The alif-lam in ﴿the imprisoned﴾ is for the known (al-'ahd), meaning: from among those whose condition you know in my prisons, for he used to cast them into a deep pit until they died. For this reason the threat was phrased more emphatically than "I will surely imprison you" (la-as-judannaka).

﴿He said: "Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾ That is, will you do that even if I bring you something that makes the truth of my claim clear, meaning a miracle? For it combines the indication of the existence of the Creator and His wisdom with the indication of the truth of the one who claims prophethood. The waw here is for the circumstantial (li-l-hal), and it is followed by the hamza (interrogative) after the verb has been omitted.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 43–45:

﴿Musa said to them: "Throw down what you are about to throw."﴾ That is, after they had said to him: ﴿"Either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw."﴾ He did not mean by it a command to them to practice magic and deception, but rather permission to put forward what they were certainly going to do, as a means of reaching the manifestation of the truth.

﴿So the magicians were cast down, prostrating﴾ because of their knowledge that the like of this cannot be achieved by magic. ﴿They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds"﴾ is a substitute for «ألقي» by badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition), or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) with «قد» implied.

﴿The Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ is a substitute (badal) for clarification (li-l-tawdih), to avert a misapprehension, and to indicate that what caused their belief was what He brought about through the hands of the two of them.

Fa-arsala Fir'awnu (﴿فَأرْسَلَ فِرْعَوْنُ﴾): when he was informed of their departure by night (sarahum).
Fi l-madaʾini ḥashirin (﴿فِي المَدائِنِ حاشِرِينَ﴾): the troops, to pursue them.

Inna haʾulaʾi la-shirdhimatun qalilun (﴿إنَّ هَؤُلاءِ لَشِرْذِمَةٌ قَلِيلُونَ﴾): on the presumption of speech (ʿalā irādat al-qawl). He belittled them, though they were six hundred and seventy thousand in relation to his troops, for it is narrated that he set out with a vanguard of seven hundred thousand. The shirdhimah is a small group, and from it comes thawbun sharadhimu, meaning a garment that has decayed and become torn. The word qalilun is used in view of the fact that they were tribes, each tribe being small.

Wa-innahum la-na la-ghaʾiẓun (﴿وَإنَّهم لَنا لَغائِظُونَ﴾): surely they are doing what enrages us.

Wa-inna la-jamiʿun ḥadhirun (﴿وَإنّا لَجَمِيعٌ حاذِرُونَ﴾): surely we are a host whose custom is caution and the exercise of prudence in affairs. He first pointed to the absence of anything that would prevent their pursuit, namely their might, and then to the certainty of what calls him to it, namely their extreme enmity, and the necessity of vigilance regarding them, urging himself to it. Alternatively, he made this excuse to the people of the cities, lest it be supposed of him what would break his authority. Ibn ʿAmir, through the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, and the Kufans read ḥadhirun. The first (ḥadhirun, with the form indicating permanence) denotes stability, and the second (ḥadhirun, the form indicating renewal) denotes recurrence. It is said that al-ḥadhir means one who is fully armed, and this too derives from ḥadhar, since such arming is done out of caution. It was also read ḥadirun with the unpointed dal (ḥādirūn), meaning strong, as the poet said:

I love the wicked boy for the sake of his mother,
and I hate him for her hatred, and he is ḥādir.

Or it means fully equipped with weapons, for that necessarily causes a hardiness in their bodies.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 75–77:

﴿He said: "Have you considered what you have been worshipping,﴾ ﴿you and your forefathers of old?"﴾ For priority in time does not indicate correctness, nor does falsehood become truth by virtue of it.

﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me﴾ He means: they are enemies to their worshippers, insofar as they are harmed by them beyond the harm a man suffers from his enemy. Or, the one who incites them to worship is the greatest enemy of the worshippers, and that is Satan. But he presented the matter in his own person as an allusion to them, for that is more effective in counsel than explicit statement, and it conveys that it is a piece of advice with which he began with himself so that it would be more likely to be accepted. The singular "enemy" (ʿaduww) is used because it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar) or carries the sense of a relative adjective (nisba). ﴿Except the Lord of the worlds﴾ This exception is either disconnected (munqaṭiʿ) or connected (muttaṣil), on the basis that the pronoun refers to every deity they worshipped, and among their forefathers there were those who worshipped God.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 78–79:

﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me.﴾ Because He guides every creature to what it was created for, of the affairs of livelihood (ma'ash) and of the Hereafter (ma'ad), as He said: ﴿And Who determined and then guided.﴾ This is a guidance graduated (mudrajah) from the beginning of its bringing into existence to the end of its term, by which it is enabled to attract benefits and repel harms. Its beginning, with regard to the human being, is the guidance of the fetus to suck the menstrual blood from the womb, and its end is the guidance to the path of Paradise and the enjoyment of its delights. The fa' (fa) is for causation (sababiyyah) if the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is taken as a subject (mubtada'), and for conjunction (atf) if it is taken as a description of "Lord of the worlds" (Rabb al-'alamin). Thus the variation in construction is due to the precedence of creation and the continuity of guidance. And His saying:

﴿And Who it is who feeds me and gives me drink.﴾ According to the first reading, it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, the preceding context indicating it, and likewise the two that follow. The repetition of the relative pronoun in both readings serves to indicate that each of the attributes (silat) independently necessitates the ruling.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 99–102:

﴿And none led us astray except the criminals.﴾ ﴿So we have no intercessors.﴾ As the believers have intercessors from among the angels and the prophets.

﴿Nor any close friend.﴾ For on that Day, "the close friends will be enemies to one another, except the righteous" (﴿43:67﴾). Or: "So we have no intercessors, nor any true friend of those whom we count as intercessors and friends." Or: "We have fallen into a ruin from which no intercessor or friend can rescue us." He used the plural for "intercessor" and the singular for "ṣadīq" (true friend) because intercessors are usually many while true friends are few. Or because one true friend strives more than many intercessors do. Or because "ṣadīq" is applied to the plural, as in "ʿadūw" (enemy), since it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar), like "ḥanīn" (yearning) and "ṣahīl" (neighing).

﴿Then if only we had a return.﴾ This is a wish for a return to the world, in which "law" (lawa, "if only") is used in place of "layta" ("would that"), since the two meet in meaning in terms of the sense of desire. Or it is a conditional sentence whose response has been omitted. ﴿Then we would be among the believers.﴾ This is the response to the wish, or it is coordinated with "karra" (a return), meaning: "If only we had the chance to return, then we would be among the believers."

﴿Indeed in that﴾ i.e., in what has been mentioned of the story of Ibrahim (Abraham). ﴿is surely a sign﴾, a proof and an admonition for whoever wishes to gain insight through it and take heed. ﴿They said: "Shall we believe you, when the lowest (al-arhalun) follow you?"﴾ The lowest (al-arhalun) are those least in standing and wealth. Qur'anic quotations: "He said: 'And what is my knowledge of what they used to do?'"

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 127:

﴿And I do not ask you any wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ The repetition of this phrase at the head of each of these narratives indicates that the mission (al-ba'tha) is confined to calling to knowledge of the truth (al-haqq) and to obedience in what brings the one who is called closer to its reward and keeps him far from its punishment. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 128–131:

﴿Do you build on every high place a landmark, sporting?﴾ "Every high place" means every elevated place; from this comes "ri'* al-ard" (a high ground), because of its elevation. ﴿A landmark﴾ means a sign for travellers. ﴿Sporting﴾ means in building it, since they used to be guided by the stars on their journeys, so they had no need of it; or [it means] dovecotes; or a building they gather at in order to mock those who pass by them; or palaces in which they take pride.

﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses﴾ means water-reservoirs (ma'akhidh al-ma'): and it has been said [it means] lofty palaces and strongholds. ﴿So that you may dwell forever﴾ means that you may make their construction firm.

﴿And when you seize [by force]﴾ with a sword or a whip. ﴿When you seize, you seize as tyrants﴾ meaning domineering, oppressive, without mercy, without intent of discipline, and without consideration of the consequence.

﴿So fear God﴾ by abandoning these things. ﴿And obey me﴾ in what I call you to, for it is more beneficial for you.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 132–135:

﴿And fear Him who has provided you with what you know.﴾ He repeated it (i.e., the command to fear God) arranged after (mentioning) God's provision to them of the kinds of blessings that they recognize, as a reason (ta'lil) for it and as an alert (tanbih) to the promise of continued provision for whoever fears Him and to the threat of cutting it off for whoever abandons it. ﴿He provided you with livestock and sons,﴾ ﴿and gardens and springs.﴾ Then he threatened them, so he said:

﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ (This is) in this world and the Hereafter, for just as He is able to bestow favours, He is able to exact vengeance.

﴿They said, "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers."﴾ For we will not desist from what we are upon. The shifting of the negation from the side that the contrast would require serves to emphasize how little they valued his admonition.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 140–148:

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿The Thamud denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Salih said to them, "Will you not fear God?"﴾ ﴿Indeed I am a trustworthy messenger to you.﴾ ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾

﴿And I do not ask you any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Will you be left secure in what is here,﴾ — a denunciation of their being left in that state, or a reminder of the blessing in God's leaving them free and in the means of their comfort, secure. ﴿In gardens and springs,﴾

The singular "palm" (nakhl) is used because of its excellence over the other trees of the gardens, or because what is meant by it is other trees.

﴿And you hew houses out of the mountains, exultant﴾ (bataran) or skilled (ḥadhiqin), from al-farahah, which is vigour (al-nashat), for the skilled worker labours with vigour and a glad heart. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 155–158:

﴿He said: This is a she-camel.﴾ That is, after Allah had brought her out of the rock through his supplication, as they had demanded.

﴿She has a share of water﴾: a portion of the water, like a turn at drinking (shirb, "a share of drinking"), and a qiyt (a "share of sustenance"), meaning her portion of the drink and of provision. It is also read with a ḍammah on the shin (shurb).

﴿And for you is a share of a known day﴾: so confine yourselves to your own drinking and do not crowd her out of her share of water.

﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾, such as striking or hamstringing her, ﴿lest there seize you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ He described the day as tremendous because of the magnitude of what befalls in it, and this is more emphatic than describing the punishment as tremendous.

﴿But they hamstrung her﴾: the hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because the one who actually hamstrung her did so with their approval, and for this reason they were all seized. ﴿So they became regretful﴾ over hamstringing her, out of fear of the descent of the punishment, not out of repentance; or [they regretted it] at the moment of witnessing the punishment, and for this reason it did not benefit them.

﴿So the punishment seized them.﴾ That is, the promised punishment. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ The negation of faith from most of them in this context implies that had most of them, or half of them, believed, they would not have been seized by the punishment; and that Quraysh were only protected from a like fate by the blessing of those among them who believed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 191–196:

﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.﴾ This is the last of the seven stories mentioned in summary, as consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and as a warning to those who deny him. The recurrence of the descent of punishment upon the nations for their denial, after the warning of the messengers, and their mockery and indifference in demanding it, repels the claim that it was due to astrological conjunctions, or that it was a trial for them and not a punishment for their denial.

﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿The trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾.

﴿upon your heart﴾: This confirms the truth of those stories and draws attention to the inimitability of the Qur'an and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). For the report of them from one who had not learned them can only be a revelation from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for "the heart," if it is meant as the spirit, then that is clear; and if it is meant as the organ, then it is specified, because the spiritual meanings descend first upon the spirit, then pass from it to the heart on account of the connection between them, then ascend from it to the brain, where they are imprinted upon the tablet of the imagination. "The trustworthy Spirit" is Gabriel (peace be upon him), for he is the trustee of Allah over His revelation. Ibn ʿĀmir, Abu Bakr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the letter zay shaddah (tashdid) and with the accusative for "the trustworthy Spirit" (al-Rūḥa al-Amīna). ﴿That you may be among the warners﴾ concerning what leads to the punishment of one who does or abandons [something].(p-150)

﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾: clear in meaning, lest they say, "What are we to do with what we do not understand?" It is connected with "descended" (nazala). It is also permissible for it to be connected with "the warners," meaning: that you may be among those who warned in the language of the Arabs, and they are Hud, Salih, Isma'il, Shu'ayb and Muhammad, upon them be blessings and peace.

﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples.﴾ That is, its mention or its meaning is in the earlier books.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 197–199:

﴿Is it not a sign for them﴾ as to the soundness of the Qur'an, or the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ)? ﴿that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it﴾, that is, that they recognize it by its description mentioned in their books. This is an affirmation that it is a proof.

Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿takun﴾ with the ta' (feminine), and ﴿āyatun﴾ in the nominative, so that it is the subject (ism) and the predicate (khabar) is ﴿lahum﴾. And ﴿an yaʿlamahu﴾ is a substitute (badal), or the subject is ﴿an yaʿlamahu﴾ and the substitute is ﴿lahum﴾ (as a ḥāl). Alternatively, the subject (ism) is a pronoun referring to the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa), ﴿āyatun﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of ﴿an yaʿlamahu﴾, and the clause is the predicate (khabar) of ﴿takun﴾.

﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs﴾, as it is, it would be an addition to its inimitability, or [sent down] in the language of the non-Arabs.

﴿And he recited it to them, they would not have been believers in it﴾, due to their extreme obstinacy and arrogance, or due to their lack of understanding and their disdain for following the non-Arabs. ﴿Al-aʿjamīn﴾ is the plural of aʿjamī, with the lightened form, and for this reason it was pluralized with the sound masculine plural.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 200–203:

﴿Thus We have caused it to enter⁠﻿ into the hearts of the guilty.﴾ "Caused it to enter" (aladhalnahu): We made it enter. "Into the hearts of the guilty": the pronoun refers to disbelief (al-kufr), which is indicated by His words ﴿they were not believers in it﴾. So the verse indicates that it is by God's creation. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, meaning: We made it enter their hearts, so they knew its meanings and its inimitability (i'jaz), yet they did not believe in it out of obstinacy (ʿinad).

﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾, the punishment that compels them to faith (al-mulji' ila al-iman).

﴿So it will come upon them suddenly﴾ in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ its coming.

﴿Then they will say, "Will we be reprieved?"﴾ out of regret and remorse (tahassuran wa ta'assufan).

﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ So they say, "Rain down upon us stones from the sky," or "Then bring us what you promise us" (فَأْتِنا بِما تَعِدُنا), while their state, when the punishment descends, is a request for respite (طَلَبُ النَّظْرَةِ).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 214–216:

﴿And warn your tribe, the nearest of kin﴾. Begin with the nearest of them, then the next nearest, for concern for their affair is most important.

It is related that when this was revealed, he (ﷺ) climbed al-Safa and called out to them clan by clan (fakhdhan fakhdhan), until they gathered around him. He said: "If I told you that there were horsemen at the foot of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment."

**Verses 217–220 of Surah 26**

﴿And put your trust in the Almighty, the Most Merciful﴾, who is able to subdue His enemies and to grant victory to His allies, and who will suffice you against the evil of those among them and others who disobey you. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read «فَتَوَكَّلْ» (fa-tawakkal, with the fa' before the verb), treating it as a substitution (ibdal, replacing one element with another) for the response of the conditional clause.

﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾ to the tahajjud (the voluntary night prayer, performed after sleep).

﴿And your movements among those who prostrate﴾: your moving about to examine the conditions of those who strive (in worship). This is as it is narrated that when the obligation of standing in prayer at night was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one), the Prophet, peace be upon him, went around the houses of his Companions that night to see what they were doing, out of eagerness for the abundance of their acts of obedience. He found them like the houses of wasps, because of the humming he heard from them in the remembrance of God and the recitation of the Qur'an. Or it means your turning among those who pray, with standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, when you lead them. God described him by His knowledge of his state, by which he deserves His guardianship, after describing him as one whose nature is to subdue his enemies and grant victory to his allies, in order to confirm trust in Him and to reassure his heart concerning it.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of what you say, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what you intend.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verses 221–223:

﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ ﴿They descend upon every lying sinner.﴾ When he had shown that the Qur'an cannot be something the devils have brought down, he confirmed this by showing that Muhammad ﷺ cannot be one upon whom they descend, for two reasons. The first is that they descend only upon a wicked, lying, very sinful person, for the connection of a human being with the unseen realms is due to the affinity and mutual affection between them, and the condition of Muhammad ﷺ is contrary to that. The second is His saying:

﴿They give ear, and most of them are liars.﴾ That is, the lying sinners give ear to the devils, so they receive from them conjectures and indications because of the deficiency of their knowledge, and they add to them, according to their imaginings, things that most of which do not agree with reality, as came in the hadith: "The jinn snatches the word, then drops it into the ear of his friend (walī), and he adds to it more than a hundred lies."

(And not) so with Muhammad ﷺ, for he reported many unseen matters, countless in number, and all of them matched reality. The word "most" (akthar) has been interpreted as "all" (kull) by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿every lying sinner⁠﴾. The more apparent view is that the majority is with regard to their statements, in the sense that few of them speak the truth in what they relate from the jinn. It has also been said that the pronouns refer to the devils, meaning: they give ear to the higher assembly before they are pelted, and so they snatch from them some of the unseen matters and inspire them to their allies; or they convey what they heard from them to their allies, and most of them are liars in what they inspire to them, since they do not convey it in the manner in which the angels spoke it, owing to their wickedness, or owing to the deficiency of their understanding, their retention, or their conveying.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 224–226:

﴿And the poets—those who go astray follow them.﴾ The followers of Muhammad (ﷺ) are not like that. This is a new sentence (istinaf) which negates his (ﷺ) being a poet, and confirms it with His words:

﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley, and that they say what they do not do?﴾ Because most of their premises are imaginings with no reality, and most of their words are in amorous prelude (nasib) with the sacred women (al-hurum), in ghazal (love poetry), in ibtihar (vehement, shameless speech), in tearing apart people's honour, in defaming lineages, in empty promises, in false boasting, and in praising one who does not deserve it and exaggerating about him. To this He pointed with His words:

﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾ It seems that, since the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an is from the side of both its wording and its meaning, and they (the disbelievers) had disparaged its meaning by claiming it is something the devils brought down, and its wording by claiming it is of the same kind as the speech of the poets, He spoke about both aspects and clarified the Qur'an's incompatibility with them, and the contrast between the state of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the state of their masters. Nafi' read ﴿yattabi'uhumu﴾ with light emphasis (takhfif), and it was also read with emphasis (tashdid) and with a sukun on the 'ayn (ta'hkin), assimilating one part to another.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 26, verse 227:

﴿Except those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged.﴾ This is an exception for the believing righteous poets who remember Allah often, and most of whose poetry is about monotheism (tawhid), praising Allah the Exalted, and urging obedience to Him. Even if they utter satire (hajw), they intend by it to defend themselves against those who satirized them and to confront the satirists of the Muslims, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawaha, Hassan ibn Thabit, and the two Kaabs. The Prophet, may peace and blessings be upon him, used to say to Hassan, «Recite, and the Holy Spirit is with you.»

(And on the authority of Kaʿb ibn Malik, that the Prophet, may peace and blessings be upon him, said to him, «Satirize them, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, it is more painful to them than arrows.»)

﴿And those who have done wrong will know what [sort of] return they will be returned to.﴾ This is a severe threat, both by virtue of what is contained in "will know" of eloquent warning, and by the generality and absoluteness of "those who have done wrong," and by the vagueness and magnification in "what [sort of] return they will be returned to," i.e., after death. Abu Bakr recited it to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, when he appointed him (as caliph) (p-153) to it. It has also been read as «ayya munfalatin yanfalituna», from al-infilat (escape), which means salvation. The meaning is that the wrongdoers hope to escape the punishment of Allah, but they will come to know that they have no way of escape whatsoever.

From the Prophet ﷺ: «Whoever recites Surat al-Shuʿara, he will have ten good deeds recorded for him for each number of those who believed in Noah and those who denied him, Hud, Salih, Shuʿayb, and Ibrahim, and for each number of those who denied Jesus and believed in Muhammad, upon them all be peace.»
